transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for seeing me. Um, well, what brings me in... it’s honestly been building up for a while now, and I just reached a point where I thought, okay, I need to talk to somebody. Because I just feel like... I don't know, like I can’t settle in my own body anymore. 

It’s this constant, uncomfortable feeling, and it’s really getting in the way of my day-to-day life. Since I'm not working right now, I handle pretty much all of the home administration, but whenever I’m supposed to just sit quietly and, you know, handle the paperwork—like the bills, or insurance stuff, or even just sitting down to go over shared household plans for the week—I just can't do it. 

I mean, I try, I really do. I’ll sit down at the kitchen table with my planner and my coffee, but the second I have to actually sit still and look at it, my skin just crawls. I end up getting up to wipe down the counters, or I just start pacing around the kitchen island because sitting there feels physically unbearable. And it's so frustrating because I have a college degree, I know how to do these things, but lately, just the expectation of sitting quietly to do those basic household plans makes me want to jump out of my skin. I just can't get comfortable no matter how I sit or what I do, and it's exhausting. So, yeah, that’s... that's what made me finally call your office.
Are you currently taking, or have you recently started, any antipsychotic medication or other new prescription drug?

Antipsychotics? Oh, no, no, definitely not. I haven't... I mean, I'm not taking anything like that at all. Actually, I haven't started any new prescription drugs recently either. Honestly, I haven't been to a doctor to get a prescription for much of anything in a really long time. I think the last thing I took was maybe an antibiotic for a sinus infection like two or three years ago? It was one of those really stubborn ones that just wouldn't go away, but anyway, as far as daily medications or anything for my mental health, no. 

I don't even really like taking medication unless I absolutely have to, you know? I mean, I'll take an Advil if I have a really bad headache, or sometimes I'll take an over-the-counter allergy pill in the spring because the pollen around our house gets just completely out of control—we have these big trees that just coat the driveway and the cars in this thick yellow dust—but that’s really it. I do try to take a multivitamin, but if I'm being completely honest, I usually forget. I'll leave the bottle right next to the coffee maker so I see it first thing in the morning, and I still somehow manage to walk right past it half the week. So, yeah, no, no antipsychotics or any new prescriptions at all. Just me, trying to manage everything on my own until, well, until I finally made this appointment.

When you feel this need to get up and move, is it also accompanied by a lot of worried or racing thoughts running through your mind, or is it more just a physical, restless urge to move without particular worries attached to it?

Um, no, it's not really... I wouldn't say I'm worried about anything in those moments. It’s actually kind of strange, because you’d think with all that pacing and getting up there’d be some big crisis on my mind, but there really isn't. It's not like I'm sitting there spinning out about, you know, the state of the world or stressing over whether I paid the electric bill on time. Honestly, my mind isn't racing with worst-case scenarios or anything like that. It’s really just this... this intense, purely physical thing. Like my muscles are just buzzing or humming under the surface. 

I remember trying to explain it to my husband just the other night. We were trying to sit down and watch this new detective show he really likes, and I wasn't anxious at all—I was actually really interested in the story! But my legs just felt like they had springs in them. I kept shifting on the couch, bouncing my knee, adjusting all the throw pillows, and eventually I just had to get up and start folding a basket of laundry in the living room while we watched. Because sitting still just felt like... I don't know, like trying to hold my breath underwater. You can only do it for so long before your body just forces you to gasp for air, you know? That's what the moving feels like. 

So, yeah, it’s definitely not a worried mind. My brain can be perfectly fine and calm, but my body just completely refuses to stay put. It's just this overwhelming physical urge to move around, even when I'd really, really rather just be resting.
Has this kind of restlessness and difficulty sitting still been a pattern for you since childhood, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

Um, well, honestly... if I really think about it, it's definitely not a new thing. Not at all. It’s funny you ask that because looking back, this was already a huge part of who I was way back in elementary school. I was absolutely that girl in class. You know, the one with the incredibly messy desk where everything was just shoved in—like, crumpled up worksheets and lost folders and broken crayons just jammed in there so tightly that things would spill out onto the floor when I lifted the top. 

And the permission slips! Oh my gosh, I can't tell you how many times my parents had to scramble because I’d forgotten to bring home a permission slip, or my mom would find it crumpled at the absolute bottom of my backpack three weeks after the field trip had already happened. I was just constantly losing track of those things. 

But as for the moving around part... yeah, my parents used to really dread parent-teacher conferences. Because there were always notes from my teachers, pretty much every single year, saying that I talked out of turn, or that I was constantly disrupting the class because I just seemed completely unable to stay seated. Like, I'd be up sharpening my pencil five times a lesson, or getting up to throw away a tiny scrap of paper, or just kind of hovering over my chair instead of actually sitting in it. I remember my third-grade teacher actually put a piece of tape on the floor around my desk and told me I couldn't cross the tape line during quiet reading time. Which, of course, just made me want to move even more, because being told to sit still is almost physically painful for me. 

So, yeah, to answer your question, this isn't just an adult thing that started recently. It’s been happening for as long as I can remember, even way back when I was a little kid. I just sort of thought I would eventually grow out of it, you know? You always hear about kids having too much energy and then they grow up and settle down. But here I am at 41, still feeling like I need to pace the kitchen island just to look at a piece of mail. It's just always been there.
Aside from the restlessness, do you currently have ongoing trouble staying focused on tasks, being easily distracted, or frequently losing track of things like keys, appointments, or paperwork?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. The distraction and the losing things... it's just constant. It's honestly exhausting. Like, just the other day, I spent a solid twenty minutes looking for my car keys, tearing the house apart, checking the pockets of jackets I hadn't worn in weeks, looking in the refrigerator—because yes, I have actually left them in there before when I was putting away groceries—only to find them sitting right on top of the washing machine. Why were they on the washing machine? I have absolutely no idea. I must have walked past it and just set them down without even registering it. 

And appointments? If I don't put it in my phone calendar the exact second I make it, with at least two alarms set—one for the day before and one for two hours before—it basically doesn't exist. I missed a dentist appointment last month because I wrote it on a sticky note, stuck it to the fridge, and then somehow it just became part of the background noise of the kitchen. I looked at that fridge every single day and my brain just completely filtered out that neon pink square. 

But the focus part... that might be the most frustrating thing of all, honestly. Because it's not like I don't want to pay attention. I really do. But I can sit down with, say, a planning email for the PTA, or even just a chapter of a book I actually really want to read, and I'll start out totally fine. I'm reading the words, I'm following along, and then... I don't know, a few minutes go by, and suddenly I'm staring at the exact same paragraph, my eyes are moving over the sentences, but I'm realizing absolutely none of it went in. Nothing. My brain just took a complete detour. I'll realize I've been thinking about whether I need to buy more laundry detergent, or remembering a conversation I had with my neighbor three days ago, or just wondering why birds don't get cold feet in the winter. And then I have to go back and re-read the whole page, and sometimes it happens again! It’s like my brain just refuses to stay on the track I put it on, no matter how hard I try to force it. It just constantly wanders off.
